content.text: A cache is a second copy of your data, and copies drift. A cached read can be stale by design until the entry expires or is invalidated, every server's in-memory cache is one more copy, and plain cache-aside has a race in which a slow reader writes an old value back after the writer invalidated it. Decide how stale each value may be, keep a TTL as the backstop, and use versions where a stale value does real harm.

A merchant raises a product's price from 80 to 100 and saves. The admin screen shows 100. For the next five minutes, some shoppers still see 80 on the product page, then pay 100 at checkout, which reads the database. The team checks the code: every save removes the product's cache key, exactly as the cache-aside pattern says. The stale price showed up anyway, and only under real traffic.
The common misconception
The belief: adding a cache is a pure performance win. It returns the same data, just faster, so it can't change what users see.

It's a reasonable belief. Microsoft's caching guidance opens with the upside: "Caching can dramatically improve performance, scalability, and availability." For data that rarely changes, it really is close to free. In development, with one user clicking one page at a time, the cache never serves anything wrong, and invalidation code that removes the key on every save looks complete.

Engineers have long known better, though. Martin Fowler's bliki keeps a favorite saying attributed to Phil Karlton: "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things."
What actually happens
A cache is a snapshot
Microsoft's guidance puts it plainly: "Think of a cache as a snapshot of the original data at some point in the past." From the moment a value is cached, the database can move on without it. A
TTL

bounds how long a stale copy can live, and choosing it is a trade: "If you make it too short, objects expire too quickly and you reduce the benefits of using the cache. If you make the period too long, you risk the data becoming stale."
Every server holds its own copy
An in-memory cache such as
IMemoryCache

is private to one process. With several instances behind a load balancer, "each application instance has its own independent cache that holds its own copy of the data", and the same query on two instances can return different results. A save handled by server A removes A's entry only; server B keeps serving its copy until it expires. A shared cache such as Redis removes that particular problem, but not the next one.
Invalidate on write still leaves windows
Cache-aside

says: read from the cache, load from the database on a miss and store the result, and on a write update the database and then remove the cached entry. Microsoft is honest about what that buys: "The Cache-Aside pattern doesn't guarantee consistency between the data store and the cache." Even in the right order, "Between the write and the next read, a reader can experience a cache miss or briefly see stale data."
The race: an old value written back
The window can last for the whole TTL. Here is the
race condition
behind the price bug:

items.text: A shopper's request misses the cache and loads the product: price 80.
Before that request stores it, the merchant's save commits price 100.
The save removes the cache key. Nothing is cached yet, so there's nothing to remove.
The shopper's request finishes and stores 80. The database says 100; the cache says 80 until the entry expires.

content.text: Facebook's memcache paper calls this a stale set: "A stale set occurs when a web server sets a value in memcache that does not reflect the latest value that should be cached. This can occur when concurrent updates to memcache get reordered." Nothing in the cache-aside code prevents it, because the read and the write-back aren't one step.
The fix: let the newer version win

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: Every product row carries a version that increases on each save, and both sides now offer their copy instead of blindly setting or removing it. The writer stores the version it just saved, the reader stores the version it loaded, and whichever is newer stays, in either order. The shopper's late 80 (version 1) arrives after the merchant's 100 (version 2) and is rejected. Offering the same version twice changes nothing, so the operation stays safe to repeat; Facebook chose deletes over updates for that reason and closed the race with leases instead.

The trade-offs are real. The writer must know the new version, usually from a version column the database maintains. One lock serializes every cache write in the process, which suits low write volumes. If memory pressure evicts the newer entry before the old one arrives, the window opens again, which is why the TTL stays. And across servers a process lock means nothing: with Redis the compare must happen in the cache itself, for example with the
WATCH
MULTI
EXEC
transactions Microsoft describes, which Redis discards "If any watched key changes before the transaction starts".

The new value right after a successful write
Old copies can't replace newer ones
Versions and an atomic compare in the cache

blocks.title: Removing the key first makes it worse

content.text: Order matters even in plain cache-aside. Microsoft: "Update the data store before removing the item from the cache." Remove it first and a read that slips in between reloads the old row and puts it back, so the stale value lives for a full TTL.

blocks.title: Give each value a staleness budget

content.text: Microsoft's advice: "decide how much staleness your application can tolerate and set time-to-live (TTL) values accordingly. For data that must be current, use shorter TTLs or bypass the cache entirely". A price on a product page may be a minute old; the price you charge at checkout should come from the database.

blocks.title: Stale data is not the same as a stampede

content.text: A cache stampede, where many requests miss the same key at once and all rebuild it, is a load problem, not a correctness one. The article on
HybridCache
and
IMemoryCache
covers it.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: List what you cache and how stale it may be

content.text: For each cached value, write down who reads it and how old it may safely be. That number becomes its TTL.

items.title: Check every path that changes the data

content.text: Make sure each write updates the database before touching the cache, and find writers that bypass your code, such as jobs, other services or manual fixes.

items.title: Close the race where staleness hurts

content.text: For values where an old copy causes real damage, add a version and let only newer versions into the cache, with the compare done atomically.

items.title: Read critical values from the source

content.text: Keep decisions that move money or stock on the database, and keep a TTL on every cache entry as the last line of defense.
Key takeaways

items.text: A cache is a second copy of your data; staleness is its normal state, bounded only by expiry and invalidation.
Each server's in-memory cache is its own copy, so a write on one server doesn't reach the others.
Cache-aside has a race: a slow reader can write an old value back after the writer removed the key.
Version-guarded writes let the newer copy win in either order, at the cost of versions and an atomic compare.
Give every cached value a staleness budget and a TTL, and read critical values from the source.
